# The Heat Is a Design Problem: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Extreme heat kills more people in the United States each year than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined, and the toll is rising as climate change pushes summer temperatures into new territory. Yet the danger is not distributed evenly across a city. On a hot afternoon, the temperature difference between a leafy neighborhood and a treeless one can exceed ten degrees Fahrenheit, and the difference between a shaded sidewalk and a sun-baked one can be measured in whether an elderly resident can walk to the pharmacy at all. This unevenness is the key insight: urban heat is not simply weather. It is a design problem, produced by decades of choices about materials, land use, and infrastructure—and it can be mitigated by better choices. The most effective cities treat heat the way they treat traffic or sanitation: as a system to be engineered, with trees, street design, housing, and transit working together rather than as isolated gestures.

## Trees: The Oldest and Best Technology

Trees remain the single most effective tool cities have for cooling, and their benefits are layered. Shade directly reduces the radiant heat people feel; a mature street tree can lower the perceived temperature beneath it by twenty degrees or more. Beyond shade, evapotranspiration—the process by which leaves release water vapor—cools the surrounding air, and canopy intercepts pavement that would otherwise absorb sunlight all day and re-radiate it at night. This matters because nighttime heat is what kills: bodies need to recover overnight, and neighborhoods that stay hot after dark are the most dangerous.

The evidence from real programs is striking. Medellín, Colombia, planted thirty "green corridors" along roads and waterways beginning in 2016, integrating trees, shrubs, and vertical gardens into its bus and bike networks. The city reported temperature reductions of roughly two degrees Celsius along the corridors, with far larger drops in perceived temperature under the canopy. Singapore, facing a tropical climate with no relief even at night, has made tree canopy a national planning priority, requiring greenery in new developments and measuring its "green cover" as carefully as its GDP. In the United States, the pattern is also visible in reverse: studies of formerly redlined neighborhoods in Richmond, Virginia, and Baltimore have found that areas denied mortgage investment in the 1930s—where pavement replaced canopy and public investment lagged—remain five to ten degrees hotter than wealthier, greener districts today.

The lesson is that tree planting must be targeted, not decorative. Cities that scatter trees evenly, or that prioritize commercial corridors for beautification, miss the point. The right approach is triage: map surface temperatures, identify the hottest and most vulnerable blocks, and plant there first, prioritizing large-canopy species that survive decades rather than ornamental trees that fit in a sidewalk grate.

## Street Design: Fighting the Asphalt Problem

Trees work only if the street gives them room to grow, and street design itself is a cooling instrument. The urban heat island effect is largely a materials problem: asphalt and dark roofs absorb up to 95 percent of incoming sunlight and release it slowly, while wide, multi-lane roads multiply the surface area doing the absorbing. Cities can fight back in several ways.

Los Angeles has pioneered "cool pavements"—coatings that reflect rather than absorb sunlight—on hundreds of miles of streets, and Phoenix has tested similar coatings in its hottest neighborhoods. The results are real but modest: a degree or two of surface cooling, though pedestrians sometimes feel more reflected heat at midday, which is a genuine tradeoff. More promising is the reduction of asphalt itself. Paris has removed parking spaces and converted the riverfront highway along the Seine to a pedestrian park, replacing heat-absorbing asphalt with people, shade, and water. Barcelona's "superblocks" reclaim interior streets from cars, creating shaded plazas and play spaces inside residential blocks. These projects do double duty: they cool the street and they make it walkable, which changes how people experience heat. A fifteen-minute walk through shade is bearable; the same walk along a six-lane arterial is not.

Street design also includes the unglamorous infrastructure of shade: bus shelters, canopies, awnings, and water fountains. Seville, Spain, has installed shade sails over plazas and, in its landmark Metropol Parasol structure, built one of the largest wooden shade structures in the world. Cities that treat shade as a public utility—something every resident is entitled to, like a crosswalk—consistently outperform those that treat it as an amenity.

## Housing: Where Heat Actually Kills

Most heat deaths happen indoors, in homes that trap heat and lack air conditioning. This makes housing policy heat policy. The first priority is retrofitting: white or reflective roofs, which can reduce indoor temperatures dramatically, are among the cheapest interventions available. New York City's CoolRoofs program has coated millions of square feet of rooftops, and India's Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan, the first in South Asia, combined cool-roof pilots with early-warning systems and has been credited with saving over a thousand lives per year. Insulation cuts both ways—keeping heat out in summer and in during winter—and programs that pair insulation with air sealing deliver the largest health benefits per dollar.

Building codes matter even more than retrofits. Cities that mandate reflective roofs, exterior shading, cross-ventilation, and ceiling fans in new construction bake resilience into the housing stock for decades. Some cities are going further by requiring landlords to provide cooling, treating it as they do heat: a habitable-condition obligation rather than a luxury. This is contentious, because air conditioning raises energy demand and can strain the grid during heat waves, but the answer is not to leave poor residents without cooling—it is to pair cooling requirements with efficient heat pumps, better building envelopes, and cleaner electricity.

## Public Transit: The Exposure Problem

For residents without cars, transit is the difference between reaching a cooling center and staying home in a hot apartment. Yet transit is often the most heat-exposed part of daily life: waiting fifteen minutes at a bus stop with no shade, no seating, and no water can be dangerous for older riders and people with chronic illness. Cities can fix this cheaply. Los Angeles, after years of advocacy, has committed to building thousands of shade structures at bus stops, and studies of its ridership show that shade measurably increases transit use. Phoenix's transit agency has experimented with cooling stations and misted shelters.
